The question this page answers

Who is being left behind — and where are the measured gaps?

People: one population, evidence from different dates

Report an error

The latest representative survey available, the Global Findex 2021 wave (survey round; Yemen fieldwork 7 November 2022 to 9 January 2023), found that 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed had an account: 5.4% of women and 18.3% of men. That establishes a low level of account ownership and measured gaps between groups for that wave. It is not a 2026 rate, it does not explain the gaps, and it cannot be combined with other measures of access, use, resilience or geography into one “latest” number.

Explore questionsOpen evidence
What this does not establish

What this evidence does not establish

The 11.9% measure is not a 2026 rate and cannot be mapped by governorate from this wave. The 12.9-point gender difference, the 9.0-point income difference, the 12.5-point education difference and the 11.1-point age difference do not establish their causes. Administrative counts of accounts, wallets, savers, transactions or devices cannot substitute for a weighted people-level measure. The evidence base does not include confidence intervals for these subgroup values, and none are calculated here, so small differences between subgroups should not be over-read.

Method

The 2021 wave does not cover all of Yemen

The latest Yemen Findex wave excludes Al Baydaa, Al Jawf, Mareb, Sadah, Socotra and several districts elsewhere; the source states that excluded areas represent approximately 23% of the population and that over one-fourth of primary sampling units were replaced during fieldwork. The Yemen sample has 1,000 respondents, interviewed from 7 November 2022 to 9 January 2023, and population estimates require the survey weights.

03Evidence

Account ownership: the representative measure from the Global Findex 2021 wave

Global Findex 2021 reports 11.9% account ownership for Yemen; the Yemen fieldwork was carried out in 2022–23. The value is a survey measure for that wave and fieldwork period, not a 2026 population rate. For context only, the World Bank's figure for the same wave across the 19 low-income economies surveyed in it, Yemen among them, is 35.2%; it averages very different economies and is not a benchmark or a ranking.

04Evidence

Measured gaps by sex, income, education and age — not yet explanations

In the same wave, 5.4% of women and 18.3% of men have an account — a difference of 12.9 percentage points. Adults in the richest 60% by household income (15.5%) and in the poorest 40% (6.5%) differ by 9.0 percentage points. Among adults with primary education or less, 7.0% have an account, compared with 19.5% of adults with secondary education or more: a gap of 12.5 percentage points. Adults aged 15–24 (5.0%) and adults aged 25 and over (16.1%) differ by 11.1 percentage points. Because each comparison is within one survey wave, the disparities can be described; their causes cannot be established from these differences alone, and they are not 2026 estimates.

Another view of the evidence
05What it means

How to read these figures

Population survey figures measure people under the survey design and weights. They cannot be replaced by counts of bank accounts, wallets, savers, transactions or payment devices. Those count different things.

Another view of the evidence (1)

More evidence and context

More detail on this question, each item with its own period and limits.
Analysis

Do not turn three observations into an annual trend

Official World Bank evidence gives three survey observations: a 2011 comparator of 3.7% for accounts at a financial institution, a 2014 account headline of 6.4%, and 11.9% in the latest verified wave (Global Findex 2021, with Yemen fieldwork in 2022–23). The years between them are not observed, and the concepts are not assumed to be identical across waves, so this resource does not interpolate an annual trend.

Analysis

Saving, borrowing and digital payments in the same wave

The same 2021 wave measures more than account ownership. In it, 21.6% of adults reported saving any money in the past year (95% interval 18.4% to 24.9%), 51.3% reported borrowing any money (47.1% to 55.5%) and 9.3% reported making or receiving a digital payment (7.4% to 11.3%). Borrowing is far more common than saving, and both are far more common than having an account — borrowing here includes borrowing from family or friends, which needs no provider at all. The intervals are derived by this resource from the survey's own weights; the World Bank publishes none. For the sources people borrowed from and the methods they saved by, the latest values this resource holds are older, from the World Bank's 2014 country profile: 51.7% of adults borrowed from family or friends, 15.0% from a private informal lender and 0.4% from a financial institution, while 0.9% saved at a financial institution and 4.5% through a savings club or a person outside the family. Those categories are not additive, each percentage applies to the all-adult base used by its question, and they are not subtracted from the 2022 figures above.

Analysis

Receipt is not the same as financial use

In the 2014 World Bank weighted country profile, 18.3% of adults reported receiving domestic remittances. Among recipients, 31.1% received them through a money-transfer operator, 2.0% through a financial institution and 0.0% through a mobile phone. The base changes from all adults to remittance recipients, so the channel percentages cannot be read on the same base as the 18.3% receipt rate.

System context

Activity is not a capability outcome

Global Money Week records of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) show programme activity during 2023–2025. Activity, documented output or completion, population-level capability measurement and evaluated programme outcome are four different levels of evidence: taking part in an activity does not by itself establish improved capability or impact, and programme effectiveness cannot be claimed without evaluation evidence that has a baseline and an endline. Population capability measures, such as the OECD/INFE scores, are a different kind of evidence, and this resource does not attribute them to these activities.

Other people-side evidence (2023)

Financial inclusion is not only account ownership

Account ownership is one dimension of financial inclusion; financial capability and financial well-being are others. In the OECD/INFE 2023 International Survey of Adult Financial Literacy, Yemen scored 42 out of 100 on overall financial literacy and 15 out of 100 on financial well-being. The Yemen survey covered 1,000 respondents interviewed by telephone and face to face between 11 March and 1 April 2023, and the report notes that the data were collected within a technical-assistance or regional project. The report does not establish whether the Yemen sample covers all areas or is nationally representative. These scores sit alongside — not replace or combine with — the Global Findex account-ownership measure, and neither is a percentage of people who are financially included.

The system is changing. What has reached people?
Yemen’s rules, institutions and payment infrastructure have moved faster than its representative evidence about people. The gap between the two is not an answer to guess; it is the next thing to measure.
Open this Reading
Evidence periodGlobal Findex, Yemen fieldwork 7 November 2022 – 9 January 2023
The gender gap is measured. Its explanation is still open.
The latest Findex observation shows a large gap between women’s and men’s account ownership inside a system where few adults of either sex have an account. The evidence tells us where the disparity is. It does not yet tell us which barriers produce it.

What measurement would change the decision?

Measurement priorityP0 · People
A current people-side inclusion baseline
The Global Findex 2025 edition contains 2024 observations for many economies, but Yemen's latest representative account-ownership observation remains 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed, for 2022 (from the Yemen Findex 2021 study fielded in 2022–2023). Major payment-system and reform changes are more recent. The latest published people-level values for receiving domestic remittances, and through which channels, are from 2014; the 2021-wave microdata contain these questions, but weighted estimates have not yet been produced.
Evidence needed: New representative Yemen demand-side survey or equivalent approved microdata with weights and clear coverage, including remittance receipt, channel and frequency.
Decision it would strengthen: A current population measure would allow change since the previous wave to be assessed without projecting reform results onto the population.
Open this measurement priority
Measurement priorityP0 · Payments / People
Active and repeat digital use
Administrative data show registrations, infrastructure and transactions, while historical evidence also records dormancy and one-time or imposed use; unique repeat users are not measured consistently.
Evidence needed: Administrative data from providers or payment systems, with deduplication rules, and/or demand-side active-use measures.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would distinguish registration or temporary activity from repeat use, merchant use and sustained financial use.
